svg.aria-label: How modern command-and-control hides inside normal-looking encrypted traffic to trusted services, and the signals that still give it away.
svg.title: Modern C2 hides in plain sight — and the tells that still reveal it
svg.text: C2 GOT QUIETER — SO DETECTION MOVED FROM 'WHERE' TO 'HOW IT BEHAVES'
Old, loud C2 — easy to block
beacon → 185.4.2.9:4444 (raw IP, odd port)
Cleartext or obvious. A firewall rule or a
threat-intel IP block kills it. Attackers moved on.
Detection was easy: bad IP, weird port.
Modern, quiet C2 — blends in
HTTPS 443 → cdn / api.slack / github / a CDN
• Encrypted (TLS) — payload contents hidden
• To trusted, common destinations (SaaS, cloud)
• Domain fronting: SNI says one host, real host differs
• Frameworks: Cobalt Strike, Sliver, malleable profiles
Now the destination looks totally normal.
…SO YOU HUNT THE BEHAVIOUR, NOT THE ADDRESS
1 · Beacon rhythm
Regular check-ins at an interval, even with jitter, over hours = a machine, not a human.
2 · TLS / JA3 fingerprint
The client's TLS handshake (JA3) can match a known C2 tool even when traffic is encrypted.
3 · Rarity + byte ratio
First-time/rare destination for this host; steady small out, small in = beacon, not browsing.
4 · Correlate — no single signal convicts; the SUM of rhythm + rarity + fingerprint does.
The shift: you cannot blocklist HTTPS to a CDN, so C2 detection is about the PATTERN of the conversation — its rhythm, rarity, and fingerprint — not the destination alone.
